nameStory: This peculiar fungus gets its name from its coral-like branching structure and the greenish algae that forms a crusty coating on the wood where it grows. The 'white' refers to its pale, whitish fruiting bodies that stand out against the green algal crust, creating a striking two-toned appearance that makes it instantly recognizable.
description: White green-algae coral is a small, unusual fungus that looks more like tiny white coral than a typical mushroom. It produces clusters of slender, finger-like or branching structures that are predominantly whitish with yellowish to brownish tips. These delicate fruiting bodies typically grow in groups on decaying wood that's covered with a distinctive greenish algal crust, creating a unique partnership between fungus and algae.

idTips.label: Fruiting Body
idTips.description: Small, coral-like structures that are simple or branched, predominantly white to pale colored with distinctive yellow to brownish tips

idTips.label: Growth Pattern
idTips.description: Grows in groups with individual fruiting bodies separate at the base, clustered together on the substrate

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Always found on decaying, moist wood that's covered with a greenish algal crust - this green coating is essential for the fungus to grow

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Fruiting bodies feel delicate and somewhat brittle when touched, with a smooth surface

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Quite small - individual coral-like structures are typically only a few centimeters tall

habitat: Look for white green-algae coral on rotting logs and fallen branches in moist, shaded areas of New England's forests. It requires wood that has developed the characteristic greenish algal coating, so search in areas with consistent moisture like stream sides, ravines, or dense forest floors. The fungus seems to prefer hardwood substrates in mixed deciduous and coniferous woodlands.

seasonality.spring: Early fruiting bodies may begin to appear on suitable substrates as moisture levels increase and temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Sporadic fruiting during wet periods, though less common in the driest summer months unless in consistently moist microhabitats.
seasonality.fall: Peak fruiting season when autumn rains create ideal conditions on decaying wood. This is when you're most likely to spot fresh, well-developed specimens.
seasonality.winter: Generally not active, though dried remnants from fall fruiting may persist on substrates in protected locations.

funFact: This isn't just a fungus - it's actually a 'basidiolichen,' a rare partnership where the fungus has teamed up with green algae to create a unique dual organism that can photosynthesize its own food while also decomposing wood!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small coral fungi, but the key difference is the greenish algal crust on the wood substrate - no other coral fungus requires this green coating to grow. Without the green crust, you're probably looking at a different species entirely.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being found worldwide, this species is considered quite rare in many regions and faces conservation concerns in Europe. The complex relationship between the fungus and its required algal partner makes it particularly sensitive to environmental changes.
compareHints: White green-algae coral can be distinguished from its relative moss club (Multiclavula vernalis) by several key features: it grows specifically on wood with algal crusts rather than on moss, has different spore characteristics under the microscope, and typically shows more branching in its coral-like structures. Both are small and pale, but the substrate difference is usually obvious in the field.
